synthesis.headline: Southwest flash-flood threat peaks Sunday with Moderate risk; Plains low then sweeps rain east next week
synthesis.narrative:
Flash flooding in the Southwest is still the main hazard, now in its third day, and it gets worse before it eases. Today WPC has a Slight risk of excessive rainfall over west-central Arizona, inside a Marginal area from southern Nevada and southeastern California into western Utah. Rain picks up again over southern California and the Desert Southwest this evening as a Pacific low approaches. On Sunday the risk rises to Moderate over central and eastern Arizona, western New Mexico and the Four Corners. Upslope terrain could see 2-4 inches on saturated soils, and WPC expects numerous flash floods. The highest Sierra and Great Basin peaks could get more than a foot of snow. SPC has no severe weather anywhere today, only scattered weak storms from South Dakota into Iowa, from the upper Texas and Louisiana coast into the Mid-South, and in Florida. Locally heavy rain moves along the Gulf Coast to the Florida Panhandle and up the Mississippi Valley. The East stays dry under 1032 mb highs over Wisconsin and off the Mid-Atlantic coast, cold in New England and mild in the South.

The flow aloft is fast, low-amplitude and close to zonal, with no cutoffs or block over the lower 48. 500 mb heights range from 588-592 dam over the southern Plains and Gulf to about 558 dam near the Canadian border. The northern jet's strongest core, 85-90 kt, exits off southern New England. A weaker southern-stream jet of 40-55 kt runs from the Southwest across Texas to the Gulf, carrying moisture into the Arizona-New Mexico rain. The 12Z chart shows only a weak trough near the Pacific Northwest, so the details of the approaching low come from WPC. Satellite shows a frontal cloud band up the Mississippi Valley, with the strongest convection south of Louisiana, and a comma-shaped cloud over Kansas and Iowa tied to the shortwave there. A mature cyclone is occluding east of the Maritimes.

On Monday a low forms on the lee side of the Central High Plains, bringing heavy snow to the Central Rockies and rain to the Heartland. On Tuesday its front moves east, with gusty High Plains winds and storms from the Mississippi Valley to the Great Lakes and Southeast. On Wednesday it reaches the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys, Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. WPC has Marginal excessive-rainfall risks both days, and how much instability develops is uncertain. Cooler, drier air follows as the next Pacific system reaches the Northwest late in the week. CPC favors above-normal temperatures across the whole lower 48 for November 5-9, with 70-80% odds in North Dakota and Minnesota. That fits a ridge anomaly of about +15 dam near Hudson Bay with troughs over the Gulf of Alaska and western Atlantic. The 8-14 day chart keeps the same setup, so the mild pattern looks likely to last.
synthesis.climate_context: A very strong El Niño frames the season. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.16 C for July-September, up from -0.39 C last winter. It has risen every season, though the gains are slowing, and the latest values are undated. An active southern-stream jet carrying Pacific moisture into the Southwest, like this weekend's, is typical of a strong El Niño autumn. A month remains in the Atlantic hurricane season, but NHC expects no development for seven days, consistent with the shear El Niño usually brings. Vance's remnants faded off Sinaloa earlier this week. Southeast of Hawaii, a Central Pacific area has a 40% chance of development within seven days. The teleconnection indices are a month old and are left out.
synthesis.regional_notes: No SPC mesoscale discussions are active. For Sunday, WPC also has a narrow Slight risk of excessive rainfall on Florida's Space Coast to Treasure Coast and a Marginal risk over eastern South Dakota. Isolated flash flooding continues in South Florida today. In Canada, the deep lows (976-995 hPa) are over the Arctic, Baffin Island and Hudson Bay. A compact low near the northwest of the continent is pushing a front toward the Pacific Northwest coast. Satellite also hints at a weak circulation off Mexico's Pacific coast.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 0900Z analysis for Saturday, October 31, 2026 shows a modest-amplitude pattern. The strongest feature is a cold-air high over the Great Lakes, with centers near 1032 mb over the Upper Midwest/Wisconsin area and another near 1032 mb off the New England and Mid-Atlantic coast, with a third 1027 mb high over southern Manitoba/Saskatchewan. These are real autumn highs, and the eastern pair is what wedges cool, stable air against the Appalachians and east coast. Lows are weak: a 1009 mb center near the Colorado/Wyoming Front Range with an adjacent trough, plus a 1011 mb low over the Pacific Northwest and 1010-1012 mb pressures along the California coast.

A cold front arcs from the Southern Plains northeast across the Ozarks and Ohio Valley toward the Appalachians, then bends southwest across the Southeast and Gulf Coast. Another cold front stretches from Nebraska and Iowa into the lower Mississippi Valley, and a stationary or warm boundary segment appears across the central Plains near the Colorado low. A Pacific cold front sits along the West Coast, and another front trails southwest from the Great Lakes toward the Ohio Valley. Because the chart is dense at this scale, I would treat the exact front types and endpoints east of the Mississippi as approximate.

The tightest gradients appear between the Plains trough and the cold high to the east, giving a broad southerly flow corridor from Texas toward the Midwest, and along the Atlantic seaboard where the offshore high meets the coastal front. Over the Great Lakes and interior Northeast the isobars are widely spaced, consistent with light winds near the high centers.

Lift and moisture focus along the frontal zone from the Southern Plains through the Mid-South and Ohio Valley, where dewpoints in the 50s to 60s on the warm side meet cooler air, and along the Gulf Coast front where upper 60s to 70s dewpoints feed into the boundary. Any precipitation signal would be tied to these boundaries and the Colorado low's trough rather than to the highs, which here mainly mark the cool, dry air mass.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis for 00Z on 31 October 2026 is a polar-projection chart, so the top of the frame is the high Arctic and the continental US sits in the lower third. Most of the deep low-pressure activity is over the Arctic basin and the Canadian Archipelago, with a cluster of centers from roughly 976 to 995 hPa spread across the region of Baffin Island and Hudson Bay and east toward Greenland. A tight pressure gradient wraps around the 976 and 978 hPa lows on the left side of the frame, near the northwest edge of the continent, where closely spaced isobars curve around a compact low and a front trails south and southeast toward the Pacific Northwest coast.

Over the central and eastern mainland, a broad ridge dominates. Two 1030 hPa highs and a 1028 hPa center sit over the area south of the Great Lakes and Hudson Bay region, and a closed 1012 hPa high is plotted over what appears to be Greenland, with a 1034 hPa high farther out in the northeast. Weak lows of 1005 to 1012 hPa lie over the central and western US and the northern Rockies and Plains, but the cross-border gradient looks modest compared with the packed isobars near the northwest Pacific coast.

A long cold front extends across the North Pacific from the left edge toward the west coast of North America, flagged with triangles, and another front with pennants and a warm-sector symbol runs along the eastern seaboard and western Atlantic. Several strong fronts and a 1004 and 1006 hPa pair of lows are also visible in the upper left over far northwestern North America and the Bering Sea side of the domain. The overall setup suggests a large continental ridge and a lively Pacific storm track, with the sharpest moisture and lift focused where the fronts meet the northwest coast.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 1200 UTC 31 Oct 2026 analysis shows a rather zonal, fast flow across the lower 48 with the strongest westerlies along the northern tier. Heights fall from about 588-592 dam over the southern Plains and Gulf Coast to roughly 565-570 dam near the northern Rockies and Upper Midwest, and to near 558 dam toward the Canadian border. The contour packing is tightest across the northern Plains, Great Lakes and Northeast, where the shaded wind field (a broad swath above 50 kt, with a core above 85-90 kt shown in dark maroon off the New England and mid-Atlantic coast) marks the jet streak. Its orientation is west-northwest to east-southeast, so the implied jet corridor runs from the northern Rockies across the Great Lakes and exits the coast near southern New England.

Along the West Coast there is a weak trough or height minimum near the Pacific Northwest, with heights around 552-558 dam and a closed contour in the upper left corner of the domain. This feature looks open in the sense that it sits within the westerly flow, and the chart supports no clear tilt assessment from this view alone. A second broad area of 40-55 kt winds curves from the Southwest through Texas into the Gulf Coast, suggesting a secondary, southern-stream jet. It is weaker and more diffuse than the northern one.

There are no obvious cutoff lows over the contiguous U.S. in this frame, and no meridionally stacked ridge-trough couplet, so a blocked regime is not supported. The pattern reads as progressive, with relatively low amplitude over the central U.S. and heights gradually rising toward the Gulf and Florida, where the 590 dam contour sits. The temperature field fits that picture: the dashed lines show about -10 to -20 C across the central Plains, Midwest and Great Lakes, and near -30 C or colder over the northern Rockies and the Northwest, which is cool for the season but not extraordinary at 500 mb.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
This Air Mass RGB from 13:21Z on 31 October shows a broad, cold dry upper trough over the central and northern Plains, with the deepest dry signature (orange-brown over the central and southern Plains, purple-blue to the north and west) running from the Dakotas and Nebraska southward through Kansas and Oklahoma. The sharpest purple-to-green contrast lies along the western and northwestern edge of the image, where saturated reds and purples near the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies mark very dry, cold upper-level air; the implied jet corridor follows that boundary, with a second strong gradient running southwest to northeast across the Great Lakes into Quebec.

A long, narrow band of white cloud extends from the Gulf of Mexico northward along the Mississippi Valley into the Midwest. It is a classic cold-front-and-warm-sector cloud shield, with the plume lying along and ahead of the front, and it joins a more convoluted cloud mass wrapping through Kansas, Missouri, and Iowa. That comma-shaped structure suggests a mature, vertically stacked low near the Missouri/Iowa area, and the orange-brown dry slot over Oklahoma and the southern Plains wraps around its southern and western flank. The brightest white tops sit over the north-central Gulf, south of Louisiana, where the cluster looks like the most vigorous deep convection in the frame, probably tied to the front.

East of the front, greens dominate the Southeast, Gulf, Florida, and western Atlantic, indicating moist tropical air with scattered cumulus fields. A broad orange-red region off the Northeast and Maritimes is dry upper-level air east of the trough axis, probably associated with another circulation offshore, and it deserves caution: it reads as dry, not as a stratospheric intrusion by itself. Small convective clusters over Hispaniola and the northwestern Caribbean, and an apparent weak circulation over the Mexican Pacific coast near the lower left, round out the tropical activity.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most striking feature is a vigorous comma-shaped system over the western North Atlantic, roughly east of the Canadian Maritimes at the upper right. A bright white cloud shield wraps a curved axis there, with a deep orange-red dry slot curling behind it toward the northwest; the orange-red tongue to its northwest is the compact, cyclonic-side signature consistent with a stratospheric intrusion, and the tight cloud swirl points to a mature, occluding cyclone. A long, thin band of cloud trails from it to the southwest, marking the trailing frontal zone, with a finer line of cloud farther south over the subtropical Atlantic.

Across northern Canada and the Arctic, near the top limb, broad purple and magenta tones with reddish patches mark cold, dry upper-tropospheric air. The sharp purple-to-green transition across southern Canada and the northern tier of the US is the airmass boundary, and it implies a polar jet corridor running west to east north of the border, though the RGB shows the boundary, not wind speed. Image-edge distortion limits detail above about 55N.

Tropically, a clear ITCZ cloud band stretches across the eastern Pacific at roughly 5-10N, with clusters of bright white convective tops from the Pacific coast of Central America westward, and more clustered convection over northern South America, Colombia, and the Amazon and central Brazil. The large orange-brown areas over the subtropical eastern Pacific, Gulf of Mexico, western Caribbean and subtropical Atlantic are dry, subsident air under the subtropical ridges, not stratospheric intrusions, and the Caribbean itself is mostly clear apart from small cloud patches near Hispaniola and Puerto Rico. In the Southern Hemisphere, a dark orange-red dry slot with a cyclonic curl is visible off southern Brazil and Uruguay on the right side of the disk, and another orange-red swirl sits well southwest of Chile near the bottom, both fitting mid-latitude cyclones.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
This 6-10 day outlook (valid November 5-9, 2026, issued October 30) favors above-normal temperatures across the entire contiguous U.S., with no below-normal or near-normal areas shown anywhere on the lower 48 map. The highest confidence sits in the northern tier: the darkest shading, about 70-80% odds of above normal, covers North Dakota and Minnesota and extends into northern Wisconsin and the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. Probabilities step down smoothly to roughly 60-70% across the northern Rockies, the Dakotas, the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes, and the Northeast including New England, then 50-60% across the central Plains and Ohio Valley, and Washington, Oregon, and Idaho. Odds fall to the 40-50% class along a band from California and the Great Basin through Colorado, Kansas, the Tennessee Valley, and the southern Mid-Atlantic. The weakest signal, 33-40%, covers the southern Rockies, Southwest, Texas, and the Gulf Coast and Southeast, meaning only a slight lean warm there.

These are probabilities of a tercile category, not temperature departures, so the map says how confident forecasters are in a warm outcome, not how large the warmth will be. The near-zonal orientation of the probability contours, rising steadily toward the Canadian border, is consistent with a pattern in which mild Pacific-origin air dominates the northern U.S., with the implied storm track and colder air displaced north into Canada. That reading is an inference from the temperature probabilities alone, since no height or flow fields are plotted here.

Alaska is also favored above normal, with the strongest odds (60-70%) along the eastern mainland and Panhandle and weaker leans in the west. Hawaii leans above normal, while the Aleutians lean below normal.

On persistence, the lack of any cool signal on the contiguous map and the northern-tier confidence suggest forecasters expect the mild regime to hold through the 6-10 day window rather than break down. The weak 33-40% odds across the South indicate more uncertainty there, so that is where a change in the pattern would show up first.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-departure outlook, made 30 Oct and valid Nov 5-9, 2026. Solid green contours are heights (labeled in meters, e.g. 5400 to 5880 m, so 540-588 dam) and dashed lines are anomalies at 60 m intervals, red positive, blue negative, purple zero. Reading the labels as meters, the red 150 near the Hudson Bay/Great Lakes region would be +15 dam; the label sits close to a contour and I cannot rule out a misread, but a departure of that order is plausible for a strong ridge.

The dominant positive anomaly is a broad center over central and eastern Canada, near and north of Hudson Bay, with the contours bulging poleward to roughly 5520-5580 m there. A second, weaker positive area sits over the Arctic and northern Greenland/Baffin region. The strongest negative anomalies are over the Gulf of Alaska and eastern North Pacific, centered well offshore from the Alaska panhandle (the 5220 m closed low on the contour field), and a second negative center lies over the North Atlantic east of Greenland and Newfoundland.

The ridge axis runs roughly north-south from the central Plains through Manitoba and Ontario to Hudson Bay and beyond, so the ridge is displaced to the east of the western U.S. and western Canada. A trough axis lies along the Pacific coast to the Gulf of Alaska, with tightly packed height contours (strong implied westerlies) curving into British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest. A second trough sits over the western North Atlantic.

The zero-anomaly line runs along the Pacific coast of British Columbia and Washington, then slopes southeast across the northern Rockies and Great Basin toward Texas, so the positive anomalies of the central continent do not reach the West Coast. Positive anomalies are not holding over western North America; they are shifted east and north, with negative anomalies covering the far West. The flow is not zonal: it is a ridge-over-the-continent, trough-on-each-coast pattern, though the strong gradient crossing the northern Pacific coast and the southern tier of the U.S. is fairly west-to-east.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb heights and departures chart (made Oct 30, valid Nov 7-13, 2026), with solid green height contours labeled in meters (5160 to 5820, i.e. 516-582 dam) and dashed anomaly contours at 60 m (6 dam) intervals. The anomaly labels on this plot (30, 90, 150, 120, 180) are in meters, not decameters, so they correspond to roughly 3, 9, 15, 12 and 18 dam; the labels read as larger than typical anomalies, and I would treat the exact values with some caution given how small the printed numbers are.

The dominant feature is a broad positive height anomaly (red dashed contours) spanning the Arctic and the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, extending over Greenland and southward across central and eastern Canada toward the Great Lakes. Its highest labeled values, about 150 m (15 dam), sit over the northern Canadian interior near Hudson Bay and the Arctic islands. Positive anomalies are also present across the northern Plains and Upper Midwest, though weaker, near 30 m (3 dam).

The western Canada question is answered by the contours: there is no strong positive anomaly over the Yukon, British Columbia or Alberta. Instead, a large negative anomaly (blue dashed, roughly -120 to -180 m, i.e. -12 to -18 dam) covers the Gulf of Alaska and the northeast Pacific, pointing to a deep trough just off the Pacific Northwest and Alaska coasts. The ridge core is therefore not over the northern Rockies in this outlook; the positive anomaly is displaced east, centered over north-central and eastern Canada and the high Arctic.

Height contours show strong westerly flow from the Pacific into the northern tier of the United States, with the 5400 and 5520 lines running well north along the Canadian border, consistent with a flat to slightly ridged pattern over the Plains and Great Lakes rather than a western ridge. A weaker negative anomaly appears off the Northeast coast near the Atlantic Canada margin, and another trough signal at the far upper right.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary:
Only two categories appear on this Day 1 outlook, valid 12Z Saturday Oct 31 through 12Z Sunday Nov 1, 2026: Marginal (green, at least 5%) and Slight (yellow/orange, at least 15%). No Moderate or High area is drawn. The Slight risk is a small pocket in the Southwest, apparently over west-central Arizona, embedded within a much larger Marginal area. That Marginal area stretches from southern Nevada and southeastern California across Arizona and into western Utah, and the Slight pocket is the highest category on the chart. Two smaller Marginal areas sit in the Southeast: one over eastern Mississippi, possibly reaching into western Alabama, and one along the southern Florida peninsula near the Atlantic coast.

The chart plots only risk categories, so the cause has to be inferred. The Southwest footprint is irregular and spans several states, which would fit a slow-moving upper-level disturbance interacting with the complex terrain there, though the chart itself does not show the driver. The Mississippi area is a compact north-south band, consistent with a local axis of heavier showers or thunderstorms along or near a front, and the Florida sliver hugging the coast is consistent with a coastal or onshore-flow setup. Nothing in the pattern points clearly to a tropical system; there is no coherent coastal footprint along the Gulf or Atlantic seaboard beyond Florida. Confirming any of these mechanisms would require the accompanying surface and upper-air analyses.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary:
This Day 2 outlook (valid 12Z Sunday Nov 1 to 12Z Monday Nov 2, 2026) shows three categories: Marginal, Slight and Moderate, with no High risk drawn. The Moderate area is the centerpiece, split into two red pockets over the interior West. The larger one sits over what appears to be central and eastern Arizona and western New Mexico, and a smaller one lies farther north, roughly in the Four Corners to southwestern Colorado vicinity. Both are embedded in a broad Slight risk that spans much of Utah, western Colorado, northern Arizona and parts of northern New Mexico, and that is in turn ringed by Marginal risk reaching toward Nevada, Idaho and Wyoming, with a tail extending into southeastern California.

A separate Marginal area covers eastern South Dakota and adjacent parts of Minnesota and Nebraska. Along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts, Marginal risk stretches from the Florida Panhandle and southern Georgia across the northern Florida peninsula, with a narrow Slight sliver along Florida's east coast, apparently near the Space Coast to Treasure Coast.

Because the chart shows only this single day, I cannot say whether the risk has grown or shifted relative to a Day 1 issuance. The geometry is consistent with a slow-moving or repeatedly forcing system over the Intermountain West, and the Moderate designation, which implies at least a 40 percent chance of exceeding flash-flood guidance, is notable for that region, where steep terrain, burn scars and dry washes are especially vulnerable.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: As of 400 AM EDT Sat Oct 31 2026 (valid through 12Z Mon Nov 2): Heavy rain renews over southern California and the Desert Southwest Saturday evening as a Pacific low approaches. Rain spreads north and east across the Southwest, Great Basin, and Four Corners, with 2-4 inches possible on upslope terrain, producing numerous flash floods Sunday over saturated soils. Over a foot of snow could fall on peak Sierra and Great Basin terrain through late Sunday. Monday, a lee-side cyclone forms in the Central High Plains, bringing wet weather and isolated heavy rain to the Heartland and heavy snow to parts of the Central Rockies. Locally heavy rain shifts from the southern Plains to the Gulf Coast this weekend, reaching the Florida Panhandle and northward up the Mississippi Valley by Sunday morning. Isolated flash flooding continues in South Florida. The eastern U.S. stays dry under high pressure, colder than normal in New England and milder than normal in the South.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook, issued 0755 AM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026, valid through 12Z Nov 1: No severe thunderstorms are forecast across the U.S. today or tonight.

A shortwave trough moving through Kansas is supporting showers and isolated thunderstorms from eastern South Dakota across southern Minnesota and northern and eastern Iowa. These are likely to continue through the morning into early afternoon, before elevated buoyancy becomes too weak and shallow to support lightning.

Storm coverage is expected to increase from south to north, from the upper Texas and Louisiana coast into the Mid-South. Modest buoyancy and weak shear should keep severe potential very low.

Isolated thunderstorms are possible from the western Great Basin into eastern Idaho and western Wyoming. Limited buoyancy should keep storms shallow and short-lived, though mature updrafts could produce strong gusts or small hail. Severe coverage is expected to be very low.

A low-amplitude shortwave moving into south-central Arizona this evening may support isolated thunderstorms. A few storms are also possible across the central and southern Florida Peninsula in moist northeasterly flow.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past six hours, so the Storm Prediction Center is not actively monitoring any organized convective threat at this time. The product gives no as-of time, so the status reflects only the six-hour window it covers. Mesoscale discussions are issued when forecasters see a specific short-term risk, such as a watch-level severe thunderstorm or tornado threat, that warrants closer attention than the broader outlooks provide. Their absence means no such short-term risk has been flagged in that window, not that severe weather is ruled out. Routine convective outlooks and watches remain the operative guidance for the wider risk picture.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
As of 800 AM EDT Saturday, October 31, 2026, the National Hurricane Center expects no tropical cyclone formation in the North Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, or Gulf of America over the next 7 days.

As of 500 AM PDT Saturday, October 31, 2026, the Eastern and Central North Pacific outlook highlights a broad area of low pressure well southeast of the Hawaiian Islands. The system is forecast to develop by early next week. Environmental conditions appear generally favorable for gradual development thereafter, and a tropical depression could form by the end of next week as it moves westward to west-northwestward across the Central Pacific.

Formation chances:
- Through 48 hours: low, near 0 percent.
- Through 7 days: medium, 40 percent.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary: No active tropical cyclones are currently listed by the National Hurricane Center, and no advisories are being issued. The product supplied does not include an issue time, so the date of this status cannot be confirmed.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows a rapid warming trend across 2026. The three-month anomaly rose from -0.39 C in the DJF season to +0.46 C in MAM, then to +0.95 C in AMJ, +1.39 C in MJJ, +1.80 C in JJA, and +2.16 C in JAS. The anomaly first reached the +0.5 C El Niño threshold in MAM, and has risen every season since, with the gain slowing but still positive through the latest season shown. The JAS value exceeds +2.0 C, which is in the very strong El Niño range. The product gives no as-of date, and the table does not say whether the latest seasons are observed or forecast, so treat the most recent values with that uncertainty in mind.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
Teleconnection indices (PNA, AO, NAO), CPC, data as of 2026-09-30. CPC has not updated this table, and all three series are 31 days old. Do not treat these values as current.

PNA: latest +0.12, up from a 14-day low of -2.04. The 7-day mean is -0.41, rising from -1.51 the prior week, so the pattern is moving from negative toward neutral.

AO: latest -0.26. The 7-day mean is +0.04, down from +1.73, after falling from +2.93 at the start of the window. The index has drifted from strongly positive to near or slightly below zero.

NAO: latest -0.78. The 7-day mean is -0.15, down from +0.28, and the index has fallen steadily from +0.86 at the start of the window.

These are observed summer values and weak, non-canonical signals. Treat them as directional background only, not as evidence on their own.
